title: Understanding Training, Validation, and Test Data
introduction: In machine learning we split data into parts so the model can learn, be tuned, and finally be tested on new information. This helps us know if the model will work well in real life.

sections.heading: Purpose of Splitting Data
sections.subheading: Separating data helps build reliable models
paragraphs: Machine learning models learn patterns from data. If we use the same data for learning and testing, we cannot tell if the model truly understands the problem or just memorizes the examples.
Dividing data into distinct sets lets us train the model, adjust it, and finally evaluate it on information it has never seen before. This mimics real‑world use where new data arrives constantly.

example.title: House Price Prediction Split
example.content: A dataset of 1,000 house sales is divided: 700 records for training, 150 for validation, and 150 for testing. The model learns from the training set, the validation set helps choose the best model, and the test set shows how the model predicts prices for future houses.

sections.heading: Training Data
sections.subheading: Data used to teach the model how to predict
paragraphs: The training set contains input features and known outcomes. The model adjusts its internal parameters to reduce errors on this data.
During training the model sees many examples, learns relationships, and builds a mathematical representation of the problem.

example.title: Training a Sales Forecast Model
example.content: A retailer provides last year’s daily sales numbers. The first 80% of days are used as training data. The model learns seasonal patterns and trends from these records.

sections.heading: Validation Data
sections.subheading: Data for tuning and checking overfitting
paragraphs: After each training round we test the model on the validation set. This set is not used for learning, so it shows how the model performs on unseen data during development.
If performance on validation data gets worse while training error improves, the model may be overfitting – memorizing training details instead of learning general patterns.

example.title: Choosing Tree Depth
example.content: A decision‑tree model is trained with different depths. The depth that gives the lowest error on the validation set is selected, preventing the tree from becoming too complex.

sections.heading: Test Data and Generalization
sections.subheading: Final check on completely unseen data
paragraphs: The test set is kept separate until the model is fully built. It provides an unbiased estimate of how the model will work in the real world.
Good performance on the test set means the model has learned to generalize – it can apply learned patterns to new, unseen situations.

example.title: Evaluating a Spam Filter
example.content: After training and validation, the spam filter is run on a test set of emails collected from a different month. Accuracy on this set tells us how well the filter will catch spam in future emails.

sections.heading: Data Leakage
sections.subheading: When information from the future sneaks into training
paragraphs: Data leakage happens if the training data contains clues about the target that would not be available in real use. This makes performance look better than it truly is.
Preventing leakage means carefully checking that no future or external information is mixed into the training set.

example.title: Leaking Future Sales
example.content: If the training set includes a column for 'next month sales' while predicting current month sales, the model will cheat. Removing that column avoids leakage.

practice.title: Simple Data Split Exercise
practice.instruction: Take a list of 30 numbers (1 to 30). Randomly assign the first 20 numbers to a training set, the next 5 to a validation set, and the last 5 to a test set. Write down the three sets and explain why you kept them separate.

keyTakeaways: Splitting data into training, validation, and test sets lets us build, tune, and fairly evaluate a model.
Validation data helps detect overfitting and choose the best model settings.
Test data measures how well a model generalizes to new, unseen information, and data leakage must be avoided to keep results honest.

mcqs.question: Why do we split a dataset into training, validation, and test sets?
options: To increase the total amount of data available
To make the training process faster
To evaluate how well the model generalizes to unseen data
To reduce the memory needed for the model
mcqs.explanation: Splitting lets us test the model on data it has never seen, giving a realistic measure of its ability to generalize.

mcqs.question: In the house‑price example, which data set is used to choose the best model depth?
options: Training set
Validation set
Test set
All three sets together
mcqs.explanation: The validation set is used to compare different depths and pick the one with the lowest error, preventing the model from becoming too complex.

mcqs.question: During training, which pattern of errors most strongly suggests overfitting?
options: Training error keeps decreasing while validation error starts increasing
Both training and validation errors increase together
Both errors decrease at the same rate
Validation error is lower than training error
mcqs.explanation: When the model learns the training data too well, its training error drops but it performs worse on unseen validation data, indicating overfitting.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is an example of data leakage?
options: Using only past sales data to predict current month sales
Including a column that contains next month’s sales while predicting the current month
Randomly assigning records to training, validation, and test sets
Applying cross‑validation during model development
mcqs.explanation: A column that contains information from the future (next month’s sales) gives the model clues it would not have in real use, inflating performance.

mcqs.question: What is the primary purpose of the test set after a model has been fully built?
options: To provide an unbiased estimate of the model’s real‑world performance
To tune hyper‑parameters such as learning rate
To adjust the model’s internal weights
To check for data leakage in the training data
mcqs.explanation: The test set is kept separate until the end so it can give a fair, unbiased measurement of how the model will work on new, unseen data.
